Submission received: 13 July 2022 / Revised: 19 August 2022 / Accepted: 23 August 2022 / Published: 24 August 2022 Abstract Macroalgae are invaluable constituents of marine forest environments and important sources of material for human needs. However, they are currently at risk of severe decline due to global warming and negative anthropogenic factors. Restoration efforts focus on beds where macroalgae previously existed, as well as the creation of new marine forests. Some artificial seaweed reefs (ASRs) have succeeded but others have failed; the contributions of ASRs to marine forest formation have been not fully determined. Here, we review ASRs, the benefits of macroalgal forests, threats to macroalgae, restoration, and marine forest formation to explore the current status of ASRs. The published literature indicates that ASRs have played critical roles in marine forest formation; notably, they support the establishment of submerged aquatic vegetation beds that allow ocean macroalgal afforestation. ASRs have evolved in terms of complexity and the materials used; they can sustainably mitigate marine deforestation. However, continuous reviews of ASR performance are essential, and performance improvements are always possible. 1. Introduction Most marine primary production is generated by algae and cyanobacteria, which also produce half of the world’s oxygen [1]. These producers support almost all marine animal life by generating the majority of required oxygen and food. Primary production is limited by distinct factors in oceans and on land. The spatial and temporal distributions of oceanic net primary production (NPP) are restricted by light, nutrients, and temperature; water restrictions are also present on land [2]. Temperature variation is smaller in oceans than on land because the heat capacity of seawater buffers temperature changes; sea ice insulates water at lower temperatures. The availability of light and mineral nutrients plays an important role in ocean primary production [3]. Models suggest that ongoing oceanic biogeochemical changes could trigger a 3–10% reduction in oceanic NPP, depending on the chosen emissions scenario [4]. Thus, ocean afforestation is important because it increases primary productivity. “Marine forests” generally refer to macroalgal habitats, as well as vegetated coastal habitats (e.g., seagrasses, tidal marshes, and mangroves). However, in certain contexts, a marine forest can be defined as a three-dimensional benthic seascape created by macroalgae [5,6,7]. Most modern researchers believe that afforestation involves ocean macroalgal afforestation (e.g., [8,9]). Macroalgae (or seaweeds) are macroscopic, eukaryotic, multicellular, autotrophic organisms that can reach lengths of several meters [10,11]. These major producers lie at the base of the marine food chain and support many communities of herbivores that seek refuge from predators. To prevent overfeeding by such herbivores, many macroalgae have evolved defense strategies, such as calcification and the production of secondary metabolites that inhibit herbivore uptake [12]. Macroalgae are found in coastal areas, as well as open pelagic regions of the Atlantic Ocean, Gulf of Mexico, and Caribbean Sea [5]. Pelagic macroalgae from Lagrangian ecosystems sometimes drift with winds and currents. Macroalgal distributions are often limited by tidal height [13], water clarity [14], wave exposure [15], and the extent of herbivory (for example, by sea urchins) [16]. Macroalgal forests are common in temperate and polar latitudes; laminarian kelp forests occur near the equator at depths >30 m in clear, nutrient-rich water below the thermocline [17]. Extensive Sargassum forests are common in many shallow tropical and subtropical environments [18]. Despite the wide distribution of such forests, unlike seagrasses and terrestrial plants, macroalgal forests require hard substrata (e.g., rock reefs) because the organisms lack roots that could anchor them to soft substrates such as mud or sand. Many researchers have studied macroalgal distributions and their potential for reducing atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations. Macroalgal forests dominate ≥25% of the world’s coastlines [19,20] and will cover approximately 9% of all ocean surfaces by 2070 [8]. A recent meta-analysis estimated a global C burial rate of 6.2 Tg C year−1 for macroalgae growing on soft sediments [21], corresponding to ~0.4% of macroalgal NPP; this is close to the lower limit of estimates for tidal marshes [22]. Several studies have shown that macroalgae serve as C donors; detached macroalgae are transported by ocean currents and deposited in C sinks beyond the macroalgal habitats [21,23,24,25,26]. Unfortunately, however, coastal ecosystems have been in continuous decline worldwide for generations because of climate change and negative anthropogenic factors; this decline has resulted in 35–85% reductions in the areas of salt marshes, mangroves, seagrasses, oyster reefs, kelps, and coral reefs [27,28,29,30,31]. fetched_contents.text: Global kelp forest restoration: past lessons, present status, and future directions ABSTRACT Kelp forest ecosystems and their associated ecosystem services are declining around the world. In response, marine managers are working to restore and counteract these declines. Kelp restoration first started in the 1700s in Japan and since then has spread across the globe. Restoration efforts, however, have been largely disconnected, with varying methodologies trialled by different actors in different countries. Moreover, a small subset of these efforts are ‘afforestation’, which focuses on creating new kelp habitat, as opposed to restoring kelp where it previously existed. To distil lessons learned over the last 300 years of kelp restoration, we review the history of kelp restoration (including afforestation) around the world and synthesise the results of 259 documented restoration attempts spanning from 1957 to 2020, across 16 countries, five languages, and multiple user groups. Our results show that kelp restoration projects have increased in frequency, have employed 10 different methodologies and targeted 17 different kelp genera. Of these projects, the majority have been led by academics (62%), have been conducted at sizes of less than 1 ha (80%) and took place over time spans of less than 2 years. We show that projects are most successful when they are located near existing kelp forests. Further, disturbance events such as sea‐urchin grazing are identified as regular causes of project failure. Costs for restoration are historically high, averaging hundreds of thousands of dollars per hectare, therefore we explore avenues to reduce these costs and suggest financial and legal pathways for scaling up future restoration efforts. One key suggestion is the creation of a living database which serves as a platform for recording restoration projects, showcasing and/or re‐analysing existing data, and providing updated information. Our work establishes the groundwork to provide adaptive and relevant recommendations on best practices for kelp restoration projects today and into the future. Keywords: kelp, restoration, marine, Laminariales, transplant, sea urchins, seaweed, costs, recovery, forest I. INTRODUCTION (1). The need to restore kelp forests Kelp forests, defined here as habitat‐forming brown algae in the orders Laminariales, Fucales, and Desmarestiales (Wernberg & Filbee‐Dexter, 2019), are globally distributed habitats which have declined around the world (Thibaut et al., 2005; Fujita, 2011; Johnson et al., 2011; Vásquez et al., 2014a; Blamey & Bolton, 2018; Rogers‐Bennett & Catton, 2019). The causes of these declines range from local stressors such as pollution to global impacts, such as climate change (Wernberg et al., 2019). Early and persistent declines of kelp forests in the 1800s were linked to population expansion of sea urchins, most often facilitated by the removal of urchin predators from the ecosystem (Roberts, 2007). Subsequent kelp population declines in the 20th century were driven by threats such as direct harvest of kelp or high levels of water pollution from urban areas (Wilson & North, 1983; Vogt & Schramm, 1991; Coleman et al., 2008; Connell et al., 2008). These stressors are still relevant to contemporary kelp ecosystem management but now interact with climate change, a phenomenon that has multiple consequences for kelp forests (Smale, 2020). Increasing water temperatures and marine heatwaves have resulted in large contractions of kelp populations as they are pushed past their physiological preferences and limits (Tegner & Dayton, 1991; Kang, 2010; Wernberg et al., 2016a; Arafeh‐Dalmau et al., 2019; Rogers‐Bennett & Catton, 2019). Warmer sea water temperatures have also facilitated the range expansion of herbivorous sea urchins which can overgraze entire forests and create urchin barrens, a phenomenon identified in most countries that contain kelp (Fujita, 2010; Filbee‐Dexter & Scheibling, 2014; Ling et al., 2015). More recently, temperature‐driven shifts in the ranges of herbivorous fishes are also causing similar declines in kelp forests near the warm edge of their distribution (Vergés et al., 2014; Zarco‐Perello et al., 2017). Such extensive losses have dramatic ecological and economic impacts. For instance, kelp losses have caused the closure of lobster, abalone, sea urchin, and kelp fisheries in several regions around the globe (Steneck et al., 2013; Bajjouk et al., 2015; Rogers‐Bennett & Catton, 2019). (2). History of kelp forest management Managing kelp forests and their declines has a lengthy global history. Traditionally, kelp forest management has been a passive activity whereby managers focused on improving environmental or physical conditions, for instance, by improving water quality (Foster & Schiel, 2010), limiting kelp harvest (Fujita, 2011; Frangoudes & Garineaud, 2015), or protecting species that facilitate kelp forests (Caselle et al., 2015). These methods can be successful, and low‐level exploitation in Chile, Norway, Ireland, and France have ensured that sustainable kelp harvesting continues to exist in those countries (Werner & Kraan, 2004; Lorentsen, Sjotun & Gremillet, 2010; Buschmann et al., 2014; Frangoudes & Garineaud, 2015). Marine protected areas (MPAs) have also worked to increase populations of species that facilitate kelp forests and reduce human pressures (Caselle et al., 2015). Artificial seaweed reefs in Japan’s subtidal zones have been designed with an emphasis on mimicking natural reef functions, selecting materials, and arranging structures to support seaweed colonization and long-term ecological function [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The evidence base indicates that these structures are “intentionally placed on the seabed” to support macroalgal afforestation and marine forest formation, which suggests a deliberate design orientation rather than a purely ornamental one [N1-F1]. In Japan, researchers have studied seaweed succession in both intertidal and subtidal zones by placing artificial structures, which implies that design decisions are informed by the goal of fostering seaweed establishment rather than only benthic or fish habitat [N4-R1][N4-F2].

On specific design elements, the available evidence points to structure form, materials, and deployment depth as central concerns. The review notes that ASRs “have evolved in terms of complexity and the materials used” and can “sustainably mitigate marine deforestation” [N1-F1]. This implies that design choices are not static but are adapted to improve performance over time. The IMO guidelines on artificial reefs also emphasize that artificial reef planning includes material selection, dimensions, and overall size, all of which are important design parameters [N1-R4]. In Japan, the context provided here includes case studies and regional examples, including Ashizuri in Tosa Bay, which suggests that deployments are often localized and tailored to site-specific conditions [N4-R4][N4-F2]. The review further states that ASRs have various shapes and sizes and are constructed from different materials, indicating that structural form is deliberately varied to suit deployment objectives [N1-R2].

Materials and engineering choices are adapted to subtidal conditions by prioritizing durability and compatibility with marine environments. The evidence mentions chemically inert materials that can withstand long immersion and have no negative impact on the marine environment [N5-R5]. This is directly relevant to subtidal deployment because such materials reduce the risk of degradation and chemical leaching over time. The review also notes that ASRs are constructed from different materials, which supports the idea that engineers choose substrates that balance functional performance with environmental safety [N1-R2][N1-F1]. The IMO guidelines further reinforce that material selection is part of a broader design process aimed at optimizing reef function [N1-R4].

As for how design decisions support initial colonization and attachment by seaweeds, the evidence is explicit. ASRs are described as supporting the establishment of submerged aquatic vegetation beds and facilitating ocean macroalgal afforestation [N1-F1]. This means that the design is intended to create a stable substratum that can be colonized by macroalgae. The review also notes that ASRs play critical roles in marine forest formation by supporting the establishment of submerged vegetation beds, which suggests that the structure itself acts as a “substrate” for macroalgal recruitment [N1-F1]. The Japan-specific context emphasizes that artificial structures are used in subtidal zones to study seaweed succession, reinforcing that deployment depth and placement are part of the design strategy to match the ecological conditions in which macroalgae can successfully establish [N4-R1][N4-F2].

Overall, the design evidence points to a framework in which artificial seaweed reefs in Japan’s subtidal zones are planned with material selection, structure form, and deployment depth as key elements, all chosen to support initial colonization and long-term macroalgal establishment [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-F2].

Artificial reefs influence seaweed succession and ecological outcomes by creating a sequence of colonization and community change that depends on substrate availability, disturbance, herbivory, and environmental conditions. The evidence base here shows that macroalgal succession is shaped by recruitment and succession processes, with nutrient availability and herbivory varying across seasons as drivers of these dynamics [N3-R1]. This is directly relevant to artificial reefs because they can alter the availability of hard substratum and the intensity of herbivory, both of which determine which species establish first and which dominate later [N3-R1].

The evidence on which species establish first and which dominate later is indirect but suggestive. The review notes that ASRs support the establishment of submerged aquatic vegetation beds and that macroalgae are important producers at the base of marine food webs [N1-F1]. It also states that macroalgae often require hard substrata because they lack roots, which implies that early colonizers are likely to be opportunistic species that can attach quickly to artificial structures [N1-F1]. The succession literature cited here further indicates that ecological succession is influenced by both nutrient availability and herbivory, suggesting that early succession may be dominated by species that can tolerate or exploit disturbance, while later succession may shift toward more competitive or stress-tolerant species [N3-R1]. While the evidence does not name specific seaweed species in the provided excerpts, it does establish that recruitment and succession are sequential and sensitive to environmental drivers [N3-R1].

Changes in community composition and biodiversity over time are also supported by the evidence. The review describes ASRs as playing critical roles in marine forest formation and notes that macroalgal forests can dominate large portions of coastlines [N1-F1]. It also states that macroalgal forests are common in temperate and polar latitudes and that they are often shaped by factors such as tidal height, water clarity, wave exposure, and herbivory [N1-F1]. This means that artificial reefs can alter the composition of benthic communities by creating conditions that favor some species over others. The evidence further notes that ASRs can sustainably mitigate marine deforestation and that their contributions to marine forest formation are not yet fully determined, implying that ecological outcomes can change over time as the system matures [N1-F1]. The broader ecological literature on artificial reefs also suggests that succession is mediated by the availability of hard substratum and by the interaction of abiotic and biotic factors [N3-R1].

Regarding whether reefs promote desired ecological functions such as habitat and productivity, the evidence is largely positive but cautious. The review explicitly states that ASRs support the establishment of submerged aquatic vegetation beds and facilitate macroalgal afforestation [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes the importance of macroalgae as primary producers and as a base for marine food webs [N1-F1]. This implies that artificial reefs can contribute to habitat provision by creating structural complexity and to productivity by supporting primary production. The review further notes that macroalgae can increase primary productivity and that their afforestation can contribute to carbon sequestration [N1-F1]. However, the evidence also warns that the contributions of ASRs to marine forest formation remain only partially determined, which means that success is not guaranteed and depends on how well the reefs are designed and managed [N1-F1]. The Japan-specific context adds that artificial structures have been used in subtidal zones to study seaweed succession, reinforcing that reefs are intended to generate ecological functions rather than simply to be deployed [N4-R1][N4-F2].

In sum, the evidence indicates that artificial reefs influence seaweed succession by altering substrate availability and disturbance regimes, with early colonizers likely to be opportunistic species and later succession shaped by competitive interactions and environmental stressors [N3-R1][N1-F1]. They can also change community composition and biodiversity over time, but whether these changes are positive depends on how well the reefs are aligned with local ecological conditions [N1-F1]. Overall, the evidence supports the idea that artificial reefs can promote habitat and productivity, but the ecological outcomes are contingent on design, placement, and management [N1-F1][N3-R1].

Management practices for sustaining artificial seaweed reefs in Japan include monitoring, maintenance, harvesting or intervention to prevent dominance by nuisance species, and responses to environmental stressors such as storms or sedimentation. The evidence points to a management system that is explicitly tied to the ecological function of the reefs rather than merely to engineering maintenance.

Monitoring and maintenance routines are a central management practice. The evidence states that monitoring is a key component of management approaches to seaweed harvesting, because effective monitoring captures changes in population structure through time [N2-R5]. The MDPI review also notes that ASRs have evolved in terms of complexity and materials used, and that continuous reviews of ASR performance are essential [N1-F1]. This implies that monitoring is not a one-time activity but an ongoing process used to assess whether the reefs are functioning as intended. The Japan-specific context also indicates that seaweed harvesting is regulated and that management includes monitoring, maintenance, and restoration of seaweed beds [N2-R3]. In addition, the review of artificial reef projects in Japan mentions a project that involves promotion of propagation aimed at protecting and nursing juvenile fish and seashells, which suggests that management includes active ecological stewardship [N2-R4]. Together, these sources support a management approach in which monitoring is used to detect changes in the reef system and to guide maintenance decisions [N2-R5][N1-F1][N2-R3][N2-R4].

Harvesting or intervention strategies to prevent dominance by nuisance species are also part of the management toolkit. The evidence notes that macroalgae are vulnerable to herbivory, particularly by sea urchins, and that disturbance events such as sea-urchin grazing are identified as regular causes of project failure [N4-F2]. This is directly relevant to management because it means that nuisance herbivores can suppress desired macroalgal communities. The management literature also states that monitoring is important for capturing changes in population structure, which implies that interventions may be needed when certain species become dominant [N2-R5]. The Japan-specific material further notes that kelp is harvested manually from boats after permits, indicating that harvesting is a regulated activity that can be part of broader management [N2-R2]. While the evidence does not explicitly describe all intervention strategies, it does support the idea that managers must actively suppress nuisance herbivory and other competitive pressures to maintain desired ecological states [N4-F2][N2-R5][N2-R2].

Responses to environmental stressors such as storms or sedimentation are also a management concern. The evidence notes that artificial reefs are subject to environmental stressors, including disturbance events such as sea-urchin grazing, and that continuous reviews of ASR performance are needed [N1-F1]. The review also highlights that macroalgal forests are limited by tidal height, water clarity, wave exposure, and herbivory [N1-F1]. These factors suggest that reefs must be placed and managed in ways that reduce exposure to extreme physical forces. The management sources do not provide detailed operational responses to storms or sedimentation in the excerpts provided, but the broader management framework implies that such stressors are recognized and that monitoring and maintenance are used to respond to them [N1-F1][N2-R5]. The Japan-specific context also emphasizes that artificial reef projects include propagation and nursing activities, which may be part of a broader strategy to buffer against environmental stress and rebuild ecological function [N2-R4].

In short, management practices in Japan appear to combine monitoring and maintenance with active intervention against nuisance species and with responses to environmental stressors. The evidence supports the idea that these practices are necessary because artificial seaweed reefs are vulnerable to herbivory, disturbance, and changing environmental conditions [N2-R5][N4-F2][N1-F1][N2-R4]. The management approach is therefore ecological rather than purely technical: it seeks to sustain the reef system over time by observing changes, intervening when needed, and adapting to stressors [N2-R5][N1-F1].

Some artificial seaweed reefs succeed and others fail because of poor colonization, competition, structural degradation, and other operational factors that affect long-term persistence and succession. The evidence indicates that failure is often attributed to poor design or to the inability to achieve set objectives, with succession and herbivory also being major concerns [N6-R1]. In the context of Japan and neighboring countries, the evidence shows that some ASRs have succeeded, while others have failed, and that the contributions of ASRs to marine forest formation remain only partially determined [N4-F2][N1-F1]. This pattern is consistent with the broader literature on artificial reefs, where success is influenced by site selection, design, and environmental compatibility [N6-R1][N6-R5].

A key failure mode is poor colonization. The review notes that macroalgae require hard substrata and that ASRs support the establishment of submerged aquatic vegetation beds [N1-F1]. This suggests that poor colonization can occur if the artificial structure is not suitable as a substrate or if the deployment conditions are not conducive to initial attachment. The broader ecological literature also shows that recruitment and succession are driven by seasonal variation in nutrient availability and herbivory, which implies that any failure to colonize quickly may be exacerbated by later disturbance [N3-R1]. In other words, poor initial colonization can lead to failure because the reef does not establish a functional macroalgal community before it is disrupted.

Another failure mode is competition, particularly from nuisance species. The evidence states that disturbance events such as sea-urchin grazing are regular causes of project failure, and that macroalgal forests are limited by herbivory [N4-F2][N1-F1]. This means that competition from herbivores can suppress desired macroalgal species and reduce the likelihood of successful afforestation. The management literature also emphasizes that monitoring is important for detecting changes in population structure, which implies that competition may require active intervention to prevent dominant species from outcompeting the target community [N2-R5]. In Japan, the context provided here includes harvesting and propagation activities, which may be used to manage competitive interactions [N2-R2][N2-R4].

Structural degradation is also a potential failure mode. The evidence notes that artificial reefs are subject to environmental stressors and that continuous reviews of ASR performance are essential [N1-F1]. It also states that chemically inert materials can withstand long immersion without negative impact, which is relevant because durable materials reduce the risk of degradation [N5-R5]. ## Integrated explanation of how artificial seaweed reefs have been designed and managed in Japan’s subtidal zones to promote seaweed succession

Japan’s subtidal artificial seaweed reefs have been designed and managed as ecological interventions aimed at supporting macroalgal establishment, habitat creation, and long-term seaweed succession. The evidence points to a deliberate design orientation in which artificial structures are intentionally placed on the seabed to mimic natural reef functions and support macroalgal afforestation [N1-R1][N1-F1]. In Japan, researchers have studied seaweed succession in both intertidal and subtidal zones by placing artificial structures, which shows that the design approach is grounded in a clear ecological goal rather than a purely engineering or ornamental one [N4-R1][N4-F2]. The Japan-specific context also includes regional examples such as Ashizuri in Tosa Bay, suggesting that deployments are often site-specific and adapted to local conditions [N4-R4][N4-F2].

### 1. Design: substrate type, structure form, and deployment depth

The design of artificial seaweed reefs in Japan’s subtidal zones emphasizes material selection, structure form, and deployment depth. The evidence states that artificial reef planning includes material selection, dimensions, and overall size, which are important design parameters [N1-R4]. It also notes that ASRs have evolved in terms of complexity and materials used, and that continuous reviews of ASR performance are essential [N1-F1]. In Japan, the context provided here shows that ASRs have various shapes and sizes and are constructed from different materials, indicating that structural form is deliberately varied to suit deployment objectives [N1-R2][N4-R1].

Materials and engineering choices are adapted to subtidal conditions by prioritizing durability and environmental compatibility. The evidence mentions chemically inert materials that can withstand long immersion conditions without negative impact on the marine environment [N5-R5]. This is directly relevant to subtidal deployment because such materials reduce the risk of degradation and chemical leaching over time. The review also notes that ASRs are constructed from different materials, supporting the idea that engineers choose substrates that balance functional performance with environmental safety [N1-R2][N1-F1]. The IMO guidelines on artificial reefs reinforce that material selection is part of a broader design process aimed at optimizing reef function [N1-R4].

Deployment depth and placement are part of the design strategy to match the ecological conditions in which macroalgae can successfully establish. The evidence indicates that artificial structures are used in subtidal zones to study seaweed succession, reinforcing that depth and location are chosen to align with the target ecological regime [N4-R1][N4-F2]. The review also notes that macroalgae require hard substrata because they lack roots, which means that the structure itself must provide a stable surface for attachment and colonization [N1-F1]. This implies that design decisions are not only about shape and material but also about creating a suitable substratum for macroalgal recruitment.

### 2. Management: monitoring, maintenance, and intervention

Management practices for sustaining artificial seaweed reefs in Japan include monitoring, maintenance, harvesting or intervention to prevent dominance by nuisance species, and responses to environmental stressors such as storms or sedimentation. Monitoring is a key component of management because effective monitoring captures changes in population structure through time [N2-R5]. The review also emphasizes that ASRs have evolved in complexity and materials, and that continuous reviews of ASR performance are essential, which means that management is an ongoing process rather than a one-time event [N1-F1]. The Japan-specific context adds that management includes monitoring, maintenance, and restoration of seaweed beds, further supporting the idea that these reefs require active ecological stewardship [N2-R3].

Harvesting and intervention strategies are used to prevent dominance by nuisance species. The evidence notes that macroalgae are vulnerable to herbivory, particularly by sea urchins, and that disturbance events such as sea-urchin grazing are identified as regular causes of project failure [N4-F2][N1-F1]. This means that managers must actively suppress nuisance herbivory to maintain desired macroalgal communities. The management literature also states that monitoring is important for detecting changes in population structure, which implies that interventions may be needed when certain species become dominant [N2-R5]. The Japan-specific material further notes that kelp is harvested manually from boats after permits, indicating that harvesting is a regulated activity that can be part of broader management [N2-R2].

Responses to environmental stressors are also a management concern. The evidence notes that artificial reefs are subject to environmental stressors and that continuous reviews of ASR performance are needed [N1-F1]. It also highlights that macroalgal forests are limited by tidal height, water clarity, wave exposure, and herbivory [N1-F1]. These factors suggest that reefs must be placed and managed in ways that reduce exposure to extreme physical forces. While the excerpts do not provide detailed operational responses to storms or sedimentation, the broader management framework implies that such stressors are recognized and that monitoring and maintenance are used to respond to them [N1-F1][N2-R5]. The Japan-specific context also emphasizes that artificial reef projects include propagation and nursing activities, which may be part of a broader strategy to buffer against environmental stress and rebuild ecological function [N2-R4].

### 3. Ecological effects: seaweed succession and community change

Artificial reefs influence seaweed succession by creating a sequence of colonization and community change that depends on substrate availability, disturbance, herbivory, and environmental conditions. The evidence shows that macroalgal succession is shaped by recruitment and succession processes, with nutrient availability and herbivory varying across seasons as drivers of these dynamics [N3-R1]. This is directly relevant to artificial reefs because they can alter the availability of hard substratum and the intensity of herbivory, both of which determine which species establish first and which dominate later [N3-R1].

The evidence on which species establish first and which dominate later is indirect but suggestive. The review notes that ASRs support the establishment of submerged aquatic vegetation beds and facilitate macroalgal afforestation [N1-F1]. It also states that macroalgae often require hard substrata because they lack roots, which implies that early colonizers are likely to be opportunistic species that can attach quickly to artificial structures [N1-F1]. The succession literature cited here further indicates that ecological succession is influenced by both nutrient availability and herbivory, suggesting that early succession may be dominated by species that can tolerate or exploit disturbance, while later succession may shift toward more competitive or stress-tolerant species [N3-R1]. While the evidence does not name specific seaweed species in the provided excerpts, it does establish that recruitment and succession are sequential and sensitive to environmental drivers [N3-R1].

Changes in community composition and biodiversity over time are also supported by the evidence. The review describes ASRs as playing critical roles in marine forest formation and notes that macroalgal forests can dominate large portions of coastlines [N1-F1]. It also states that macroalgal forests are common in temperate and polar latitudes and that they are often shaped by factors such as tidal height, water clarity, wave exposure, and herbivory [N1-F1]. This means that artificial reefs can alter the composition of benthic communities by creating conditions that favor some species over others. The evidence further notes that ASRs can sustainably mitigate marine deforestation and that their contributions to marine forest formation are not yet fully determined, implying that ecological outcomes can change over time as the system matures [N1-F1]. The broader ecological literature on artificial reefs also suggests that succession is mediated by the availability of hard substratum and by the interaction of abiotic and biotic factors [N3-R1].

### 4. Ecological functions and productivity

The evidence supports the idea that artificial reefs can promote desired ecological functions such as habitat and productivity. The review explicitly states that ASRs support the establishment of submerged aquatic vegetation beds and facilitate macroalgal afforestation [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes the importance of macroalgae as primary producers and as a base for marine food webs [N1-F1]. This implies that artificial reefs can contribute to habitat provision by creating structural complexity and to productivity by supporting primary production. The review further notes that macroalgae can increase primary productivity and that their afforestation can contribute to carbon sequestration [N1-F1]. However, the evidence also warns that the contributions of ASRs to marine forest formation remain only partially determined, which means that success is not guaranteed and depends on how well the reefs are designed and managed [N1-F1]. The Japan-specific context adds that artificial structures have been used in subtidal zones to study seaweed succession, reinforcing that reefs are intended to generate ecological functions rather than simply to be deployed [N4-R1][N4-F2].

### 5. Why some reefs succeed and others fail

Some artificial seaweed reefs succeed and others fail because of poor colonization, competition, structural degradation, and other operational factors that affect long-term persistence and succession. The evidence indicates that failure is often attributed to poor design or to the inability to achieve set objectives, with succession and herbivory also being major concerns [N6-R1]. In the context of Japan and neighboring countries, the evidence shows that some ASRs have succeeded, while others have failed, and that the contributions of ASRs to marine forest formation remain only partially determined [N4-F2][N1-F1]. This pattern is consistent with the broader literature on artificial reefs, where success is influenced by site selection, design, and environmental compatibility [N6-R1][N6-R5].

A key failure mode is poor colonization. The review notes that macroalgae require hard substrata and that ASRs support the establishment of submerged aquatic vegetation beds [N1-F1]. This suggests that poor colonization can occur if the artificial structure is not suitable as a substrate or if the deployment conditions are not conducive to initial attachment. The broader ecological literature also shows that recruitment and succession are driven by seasonal variation in nutrient availability and herbivory, which implies that any failure to colonize quickly may be exacerbated by later disturbance [N3-R1]. In other words, poor initial colonization can lead to failure because the reef does not establish a functional macroalgal community before it is disrupted.

Another failure mode is competition, particularly from nuisance species. The evidence states that disturbance events such as sea-urchin grazing are regular causes of project failure, and that macroalgal forests are limited by herbivory [N4-F2][N1-F1]. This means that competition from herbivores can suppress desired macroalgal species and reduce the likelihood of successful afforestation. The management literature also emphasizes that monitoring is important for detecting changes in population structure, which implies that competition may require active intervention to prevent dominant species from outcompeting the target community [N2-R5]. In Japan, the context provided here includes harvesting and propagation activities, which may be used to manage competitive interactions [N2-R2][N2-R4].

Structural degradation is also a potential failure mode. The evidence notes that artificial reefs are subject to environmental stressors and that continuous reviews of ASR performance are essential [N1-F1]. It also states that chemically inert materials can withstand long immersion without negative impact, which is relevant because durable materials reduce the risk of degradation [N5-R5]. The broader artificial reef literature further suggests that deployment failing to achieve set goals may be linked to poor design [N6-R1]. This indicates that structural integrity over time is important: if a reef degrades, it may lose its ability to support colonization and succession.

Mixed or failed deployments in Japan and elsewhere provide lessons about what works and what does not. The evidence shows that ASRs have evolved in complexity and materials over time, and that continuous performance reviews are necessary [N1-F1]. It also notes that some deployments have succeeded while others have failed, and that the contributions of ASRs to marine forest formation remain only partially determined [N4-F2][N1-F1]. This implies that success is context-dependent and that no single design or management approach is universally effective. The broader artificial reef literature similarly states that many factors can make an artificial reef a success or failure, including material choice, placement, and environmental conditions [N6-R3][N6-R5]. The evidence further notes that artificial reef success is related to position in the surrounding habitat, suggesting that site selection is as important as structure design [N6-R5].

### 6. Lessons for design and management

The integrated evidence suggests several lessons for designing and managing artificial seaweed reefs in Japan’s subtidal zones to promote seaweed succession:

1. **Design should be ecological, not just structural.** The reefs should be intended to mimic natural reef functions and support macroalgal afforestation, not simply to provide a hard substrate [N1-R1][N1-F1].  
2. **Materials should be durable and environmentally compatible.** Chemically inert materials that can withstand long immersion are preferable to reduce degradation and negative ecological impacts [N5-R5].  
3. **Structure form and deployment depth should be site-specific.** The review indicates that ASRs vary in shape, size, and materials, and that deployments are adapted to local conditions [N1-R2][N4-R4].  
4. **Monitoring and maintenance are essential.** Effective monitoring captures changes in population structure and supports ongoing maintenance [N2-R5][N1-F1].  
5. **Intervention is needed to control nuisance species.** Herbivory, especially by sea urchins, can suppress desired macroalgal communities, so managers must actively suppress competition [N4-F2][N2-R5].  
6. **Environmental stressors must be anticipated.** Reefs must be placed and managed in ways that reduce exposure to storms, sedimentation, and other disturbances [N1-F1][N2-R5].  
7. **Success depends on continuous evaluation.** The evidence repeatedly emphasizes the need for continuous reviews of ASR performance and for adapting designs and management as the system matures [N1-F1][N6-R1].  

### Conclusion

In Japan’s subtidal zones, artificial seaweed reefs have been designed and managed as part of an ecological restoration strategy. They are engineered with materials and forms adapted to subtidal conditions, placed to support macroalgal establishment, and monitored over time to sustain community development [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-R4][N5-R5]. Management includes active intervention to prevent dominance by nuisance species and responses to environmental stressors, while ecological evidence shows that reefs can shape seaweed succession, change community composition, and promote habitat and productivity [N2-R5][N4-F2][N3-R1][N1-F1]. The evidence also shows that some reefs succeed and others fail because of poor colonization, competition, and structural degradation, with the strongest success linked to good design, appropriate placement, and ongoing management [N6-R1][N4-F2][N6-R5]. Overall, the evidence supports a conclusion that artificial seaweed reefs in Japan’s subtidal zones are most effective when they are designed ecologically, monitored continuously, and managed proactively to support seaweed succession.
